TextView.android:text: Intermediate Lesson 10: The Extremal Principle & Monovariants

When faced with a complex configuration, look at the extremes: the largest, the smallest, the first, the last, the closest, or the furthest element. By analyzing the 'extreme' element, you often restrict the problem enough to force a contradiction or find a solution.\n\nClassic Example (Sylvester-Gallai Theorem): 'Given a finite set of points not all on one line, there is a line passing through EXACTLY two points.' The proof relies entirely on picking the point and the line that have the SMALLEST positive distance between them.

While an Invariant never changes, a Monovariant is a quantity that changes strictly in ONE direction (it either strictly increases or strictly decreases) every time a specific operation is applied.\n\nIf a quantity strictly decreases but cannot go below zero (bounded below), the process MUST eventually stop. This is used to prove that certain games, algorithms, or natural processes will always terminate, no matter what choices are made.

Pioneered by Pierre de Fermat, Infinite Descent is a type of proof by contradiction used heavily in Diophantine equations.\n\nTo prove an equation has no positive integer solutions, you assume it DOES have a solution. Then, using algebraic manipulation, you prove that if a solution (x, y) exists, there must be a strictly SMALLER positive integer solution (x', y'). This creates an infinite sequence of decreasing positive integers, which is impossible because you will eventually hit zero.
4. The Mean Value Principle in Logic

A beautiful logical tool: If the average of a set of numbers is 'A', then there must be at least one number ≥ A, and at least one number ≤ A.\n\nExample: If 100 people sit in a circle and everyone's salary is exactly the average of their two neighbors, then EVERYONE must have the exact same salary. Why? Because the person with the MAXIMUM salary (Extremal Principle) must be the average of their neighbors. The only way the maximum can be the average is if both neighbors equal the maximum. This spreads around the circle!

On a large flat field, there are 'n' people. The distances between any two people are all distinct. Everyone shoots a water balloon at the person CLOSEST to them. Prove that at least one person stays completely dry.

Solution: Look at the extremes! Consider the two people who have the ABSOLUTE SMALLEST distance between them in the entire field (let's call them A and B). 
Since A is closer to B than anyone else, A will shoot B. Since B is closer to A than anyone else, B will shoot A. They shoot each other.
Now, no one else in the field can shoot A or B, because anyone else (say C) must have someone closer to them than A or B (otherwise A and C would be the shortest distance, which is a contradiction). 
Since A and B use up 2 balloons on each other, the remaining (n-2) people have only (n-2) balloons left to shoot at each other. Thus, in a chain, someone must be left out. *Note: this specifically applies when 'n' is an odd number!*
Prove that the equation x^3 + 2y^3 = 4z^3 has no positive integer solutions.

Solution: Assume there is a solution. If x^3 + 2y^3 = 4z^3, then x^3 must be even. So 'x' is even. Let x = 2x'.
Substituting: 8x'^3 + 2y^3 = 4z^3.
Divide by 2: 4x'^3 + y^3 = 2z^3.
Now, y^3 must be even. So 'y' is even. Let y = 2y'.
Substituting: 4x'^3 + 8y'^3 = 2z^3.
Divide by 2: 2x'^3 + 4y'^3 = z^3.
Now, z^3 must be even! So 'z' is even. Let z = 2z'.
We get: x'^3 + 2y'^3 = 4z'^3. 
Notice this is the EXACT SAME equation, but with strictly smaller integers (x', y', z'). This process can be repeated infinitely, generating smaller and smaller positive integers. This is impossible. Therefore, the only solution is x=0, y=0, z=0.
